beats.intro: Chapter forty-four. [[sub]]How many ways can you arrange or choose things? It depends on whether order matters.
beats.order: Three friends: Ana, Ben, and Cal. [[perm]]If you pick a president and a vice president, Ana then Ben is different from Ben then Ana. Order matters, so each arrangement is a permutation. [[comb]]If you just pick two of them for a committee, Ana and Ben is the same committee as Ben and Ana. Order doesn't matter, so each group is a combination.
beats.repeat: Start with permutations that allow repetition. [[code]]A lock code has three digits, each from zero to nine, and digits can repeat. [[s1]]The first digit has ten choices. [[s2]]The second still has ten, [[s3]]and so does the third. [[mult]]By the counting principle, that's ten times ten times ten, or ten to the third power: one thousand codes. [[gen]]In general, choosing r times from n options with repetition gives n to the r.
beats.norep: Without repetition, the choices shrink. [[books]]Arrange four different books on a shelf. [[s1]]Any of the four can go first. [[s2]]Then three are left for the second spot, [[s3]]two for the third, [[s4]]and one for the last. [[mult]]Four times three times two times one is twenty-four. [[fact]]A product like this is called a factorial, written with an exclamation mark: four factorial. [[zero]]By definition, zero factorial is one.
beats.npr: Sometimes you arrange only some of the items. [[club]]A club has six members and needs a president, a vice president, and a secretary. [[s]]That's six choices, then five, then four: one hundred twenty. [[name]]This is called the number of permutations of six things taken three at a time. [[form]]As a formula, it's six factorial over three factorial. [[cancel]]The three times two times one cancels, [[left]]leaving six times five times four. [[gen]]In general, n factorial over the quantity n minus r, factorial.
beats.qp: Quick check. Arrange some of the items.
beats.comb: Now let order stop mattering. [[menu]]A dessert plate lets you pick two of four desserts. [[ordered]]Counting ordered picks gives four times three, twelve. [[pairs]]But apple then berry, and berry then apple, are the same plate. [[twice]]Every plate was counted twice. [[div]]So divide by two: six different plates.
beats.groups: Why divide by two? [[pick]]Two items can be ordered in two factorial ways. [[three]]A group of three can be ordered in three factorial, or six, ways. [[each]]Every group shows up that many times in the permutation count. [[rule]]So the number of combinations is the number of permutations divided by r factorial.
beats.q2: Quick check. Does order matter here?
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Order matters: permutations. Order doesn't: combinations. [[w2]]With repetition, n choices r times gives n to the r. [[w3]]Without repetition, the permutations of n things taken r at a time are n factorial over n minus r factorial. [[w4]]Combinations are those permutations divided by r factorial. [[end]]Now try the chapter practice.
beats.finish: Excellent. That's the end of chapter forty-four, and of unit seven.
